subject: RICOCHET anti-cheat: MW4 and Warzone, with dated supporting history and platform context

evidence_levels.V: Attributed vendor/policy statement supported by the cited primary text; runtime accuracy not independently reproduced.
evidence_levels.P: Documented platform/protocol/sample-code behavior; not evidence of private RICOCHET API selection.
evidence_levels.A: Contents of a pinned public artifact; no anti-cheat runtime implication.
evidence_levels.R: Author-reported historical experiment; preserve its test dates and limitations.
evidence_levels.O: Reproduced static contents of the hash-identified official diagnostic utility; not a game/kernel-driver experiment.

reading: Stream JSONL. Join src IDs to source records. Filter topic, level, date and scope before drawing conclusions. C IDs are primary-text findings; T IDs are official-utility static observations.

fields.at: Reviewed source paragraph IDs P####, bound to the source normalized-text SHA-256; not publisher line numbers.
fields.evidence: Self-contained artifact metadata: file, metadata/code location and observed values. File offsets refer to decompressed components. RVAs and IL offsets are distinct.
fields.date: Claim as-of date, not a universal deployment date. All source access/review occurred on 2026-10-31.

limits: Proprietary current kernel/game code and private detection rules were not verified.
Microsoft examples and historical experiments are not measurements of current MW4/Warzone internals.
Server Culling for Warzone Season 1 is an attributed announced scope, not a measured present deployment.
Source support establishes what the source says; hashes and automated consistency checks do not establish factual truth.
Published OS driver interfaces do not establish a private game inventory-write API, persistent unlock-all mechanism or current MW4/Warzone mod SDK.
CVE-2026-45642 is a documented platform flaw with a stated service-side fix; these records do not establish a current MW4/Warzone unlock-all or mod-menu bypass.
latest_pass: Online primary documents, official replies and vulnerability records only. Existing static observations are retained from the earlier artifact pass; no new executable or game test was performed.

text: Activision reports: RICOCHET combines client protection, server analytics, investigations, mitigations, and account security.
Activision’s internally developed kernel driver reports applications attempting to interact with protected games.
Activision says the driver installs automatically, starts with the game, and stops on game exit.
The FAQ requires the driver for protected PC games, without an opt-out.
The FAQ states that the driver examines machine/process interactions to identify manipulation of the protected game.
Activision reports: Protected PC titles listed: MW4, BO7, BO6, Warzone, MWIII, MWII, and Vanguard.
Activision reports stability testing across varied PCs and ongoing iteration.
Activision reports: RICOCHET was announced October 13, 2021, with backend protections for Vanguard and Warzone and a Warzone-first PC-driver rollout.
Activision reports: The driver was announced for PC; console players benefit from reduced PC cheating in cross-play, without receiving that Windows driver.
The launch announcement promises game-only driver operation and monitoring/reporting of Call of Duty-related activity.
Activision reports: The original announcement already described ML examining server gameplay data for suspicious behavioral trends.
Activision reports: The December 7 announcement scheduled the driver rollout to begin in Asia-Pacific with Pacific launch, before worldwide expansion.
Activision reports: The December 15 progress report announced global PC-driver deployment, installed through the game update.
Activision reports: Damage Shield reduces a detected cheater’s ability to inflict lethal/critical damage while leaving that player vulnerable and available for investigation.
Activision reports: The Damage Shield announcement describes a server-triggered response to detected real-time tampering.
Activision reports: Extreme/repeated violations and attempts to disguise identity or hardware identity may result in permanent suspensions across accounts/titles.
Activision reports: Vanguard’s kernel driver launched globally April 26, 2022; upgrades were staged there before bringing Warzone’s driver to parity.
Activision reports: Cloaking hides legitimate opponents, including their relevant visual/audio cues, from detected cheaters while opponents can still see them.
Activision describes both daily bans and ban waves.
Activision reports: The report says cheating bans remove the offending player from the relevant leaderboards.
Activision reports: The team spans security, game/server engineering, research, and data science and collaborates with game-development teams.
Activision reports: Mitigations constrain detected cheaters while allowing collection and analysis; bans remain a separate enforcement outcome.
Activision reports: Disarm removes a detected cheater’s weapons, including fists.
Activision reports: Some damage still registers to preserve hit feedback and indicate the attack’s origin to the protected player.
The Q&A says player reports help identify cheating trends and support investigations.
Activision reports: The team identifies stolen/replacement accounts as part of the cheating ecosystem and recommends two-factor authentication.
Activision reports: The unified security platform introduced with MWII was intended to improve detection, mitigation development, and update frequency.
Activision described moving selected processes toward server-side execution to retain authority over more gameplay systems.
Activision reports: Driver updates were described as improving prevention and feeding additional information into detection and mitigation systems.
Activision reports: The report scheduled the driver for MWII’s October 28 and Warzone 2.0’s November 16 launch dates, globally.
Activision says the MWII beta used partial protections, with full mitigations scheduled for launch.
Activision describes RIT review of completed matches using captured and stored match-gameplay data.
Activision reports: The team said it automatically captured high-tier Ranked match data and suspicious-account data across multiplayer modes.
Activision reports: Reports can flag accounts for review through tools including RIT.
Activision reports: Detection of controller-passthrough devices used to gain advantages such as recoil reduction was announced as globally deployed across platforms.
Activision reports: The published device-response sequence began with warnings and could escalate to mitigations, suspensions, or bans for continued misuse.
Activision reports: The team may adjust SR for players repeatedly benefiting from banned cheating partners, even without detecting cheats on those partners’ own machines.
Activision reports: Hallucinations are decoy characters supplied to flagged players and hidden from legitimate players.
Activision reports: They can disrupt verified cheaters or test suspicious accounts; interaction with an otherwise unseen decoy provides a detection signal.
Activision reports: The published live design cloned an active player’s movement and presented plausible player information to cheat tools.
Activision reports: Quicksand slowed/froze cheaters through connection delay and could alter inputs; it was decommissioned because the visual disruption could distract legitimate players.
Activision reports: Configurable decoys invert the usual detection race: cheats must distinguish fake entities while defenders can vary their behavior.
The Hallucinations paper reports that tested cheat programs treated its decoys as real players.
Activision reports: ML assists behavioral discovery, abnormal-account challenges, action prioritization, and replay triage. The report says ML systems do not issue bans.
Activision reports: The replay model flags suspicious behavior such as wallhacks/rage cheating and prioritizes review by the team.
Activision reports: Splat can disable a confirmed cheater’s parachute or alter velocity so a small fall becomes fatal.
Activision says player reports alone do not activate Splat and it is reserved for verified cheaters.
Activision reports: The report describes identifying more than 110,000 accounts exposed through reused credentials in 2023 and resetting them to prevent misuse.

scope: BO6 launch / titles sharing the driver
text: Activision reports: The BO6 launch plan included an updated kernel driver, new aimbot/behavioral ML, and existing mitigations.
Activision reported about 10 matches before removal in Beta Weekend One and 5 in Weekend Two.

scope: BO6 Beta overall; 25% figure is specific to Weekend Two
text: Activision reported 25% of Weekend Two bans in the first match, and over 12,000 accounts stopped before a match during the beta overall.
Activision reports: The team described using recorded Call of Duty League play to model elite legitimate performance, alongside cheating examples.
Activision acknowledges purpose-built cheating hardware beyond ordinary kernel-level software threats.
Activision reports: The vendor reported a peak of 4.4 million categorized data points per hour, used to flag anomalous play for human review.
Activision reports: The 50 multiplayer-win entry condition supplied match history for review; AFK and regional-ping checks targeted boosting/VPN abuse.
Activision reports: The team announced manual review of rename requests at Crimson rank and above and replay monitoring of top players.
Activision reports: Some detections first ran in monitoring/data-only mode before being enabled to flag accounts for action.
Activision reports: The team acknowledged that its Season 01 integration, particularly Ranked Play, fell short despite the earlier launch results.
Activision reports: The December report explicitly describes kernel-driver detections aimed at blocking memory tampering.
Activision reports: The team expanded its replay-rendering farm and human clip-review capacity, with detections influencing review priority.
Activision reports: The December report says account bans were occurring hourly at that time.
Activision reports: The January roadmap announces driver-security improvements, reinforced encryption, and a new tampering-detection system for Season 02.
Activision reports: The update identifies behavioral models, account trust, and hardware identifiers as inputs for targeting repeat cheaters.
Activision reports: The team said it did not use IP-address bans because shared networks would create collateral impact.
Activision reports: Repeated submissions from one reporter against one target are counted as one report, according to the team.
Activision reports: Accounts regularly partying with a banned cheater are flagged for investigation, supporting action against boosting.
Activision reports: LMM separates suspicious accounts during investigation; placement does not establish cheating.
Activision lists changed account behavior and improbable performance from a new account as examples of LMM triggers.
Activision reports: An LMM party member brings the party into that pool; unaffected accounts return to standard matchmaking after leaving.
Activision says spam reports add no information and can reduce reporter trust or incur penalties.
Activision reports: The team states it rolls back account action found unwarranted during system-accuracy examinations.
Activision reports: The announced SR correction system refunded recent losses to banned cheaters and could remove gains earned with them; initial lookback was two weeks.
Activision reports: The team announced extra verification on new platform-account links, with gameplay blocked on that platform if verification fails.
Activision reports: Video plus game data produces a suspicious-behavior probability score; the published workflow elevates it for human validation.
Activision reports: RIT’s main focus in this update was Ranked multiplayer/battle royale, prioritizing high-scoring suspicious clips for faster review.
Activision reported four matches on average before new cheating accounts were banned during Seasons 02–03.
Activision reports: The team reported legal demands to device/script vendors and said cheating with such tools could receive permanent bans.
Activision reports: TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot integration began as a phased test with notifications; those settings were not yet mandatory during Season 05.
Activision reports: The August update announced TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot would be mandatory for BO7 PC play.
Activision says the final boot-state verification check happens on its servers.
Activision says its boot-attestation process does not access personal files or personal information.
Activision claims no in-game-quality impact from TPM/Secure Boot startup checks.
Activision explicitly described verification of critical PC security settings through Microsoft infrastructure as Remote Attestation.
Activision reports: TPM can appear enabled in local Windows tools yet fail remote attestation because of firmware compatibility.
Activision says most detected cheaters were banned directly; more than 55,000 were disrupted with mitigations during August before permanent bans.
Activision reports: The update describes vehicles exploding for selected detected cheaters and suppressing their weapon/vehicle damage during investigation.
Activision reports: In-game Limited Matchmaking status notifications were announced as live.
Activision reports: The September report requires TPM/Secure Boot for BO7’s PC beta and announces Azure remote-verification upgrades for the November 14 launch.
Activision reports: The team announced a new generation of ML detections trained using millions of BO6 gameplay hours.
Activision reports: Anti-cheat systems were to be adjusted dynamically during the beta, with the full set of upgrades reserved for launch.
Activision reports: The Season 01 report extended the TPM 2.0/Secure Boot requirement to Warzone.
Activision reports: The wizard was announced for later in Season 01 to check configuration and provide compliance guidance.
Activision reports: Updated boosting/botting detection targeted both artificially progressed accounts and the accounts running the services.
Activision reports: The team announced stronger pre-match remote verification using Microsoft Azure Attestation, building on TPM/Secure Boot requirements.
Activision reports: The announced method analyzes input timing, consistency, and response patterns rather than relying only on plugged-in device identity.
Activision reports: The system seeks classes of machine-generated recoil/aim behavior, because device configurations can change and lack one universal signature.
Activision says the initial input-device rollout targeted common configurations and would be expanded iteratively.
Activision reports: SMS 2FA began with new accounts and planned expansion to existing accounts without ownership of a COD title from the preceding two years.
Activision reports: Recent-game ownership and SMS requirements are evaluated separately per linked platform, so ownership on one platform does not exempt another.
Activision reports: The team announced warnings that failing attestation would limit future playlist access.
Activision reports: Season 04 expanded MAA enforcement: failed/incomplete attestation routes players into separate matchmaking with limited playlists.
Activision reports: The listed access was Nuketown 24/7 in BO7 and Battle Royale Casual in Warzone; noncompliant PCs could not match with compliant PCs or consoles.
Activision reports: A noncompliant party member can cause the party to receive failed-attestation messaging and adjusted matchmaking.
Activision reports: The team acknowledges hardware/firmware compatibility failures unrelated to intentional tampering; fixes can depend on hardware manufacturers.
Activision reports that nearly two-thirds of temporarily banned scripted-device users returned to BO7 without the offending scripts.
Activision reports: The team described combined pressure on cheats, replacement/stolen accounts, evasion services, resellers, and operators through technical and legal measures.
Activision reports: The September report claims over 375 reseller operations disrupted, over 80 cease-and-desist demands, and 31 primary vendors shut down.
Activision reports: The September report says more than 70,000 new hardware bans were issued during the preceding month.
Activision reports: Technical detections seek unauthorized game interaction while behavioral systems analyze play over time to inform investigation and enforcement.
Activision reports: BO7/Warzone noncompliance can restrict modes, including Ranked, and place players in separate pools.
Activision reports: MW4 requires TPM 2.0/Secure Boot for all online modes; noncompliance blocks online gameplay.
The official wizard listing is version 1.3.0, updated October 21, 2026, for configuration/compliance diagnosis.
Activision reports: The support page associates enrollaik.exe/UAC approval with generating an authorization key and validating TPM settings.
Activision reports: The wizard distinguishes TPM/Secure Boot disabled, GPT/UEFI configuration, BIOS update, authorization-key, and TCG-event-log problems.
Activision reports: The guide lists Windows 10 22H2+ or Windows 11 and UEFI/GPT for the supported Secure Boot configuration.
Activision reports: The privacy policy permits monitoring/recording gameplay, communications, device activities, and programs running alongside a game under applicable terms.
Activision’s privacy policy covers its properties broadly and lists anti-fraud, anti-cheat, and anti-toxicity technologies together.
Activision offers a security intake leading to its private HackerOne program for qualifying vulnerabilities; player cheating reports belong in the in-game report tool.
Activision reports: Active account sanctions follow the Activision account across linked devices; sanctions can include warnings, temporary/permanent bans, Ranked restrictions, and corrections.
Activision reports: Device bans are distinct from account bans, can cover multiple titles, can vary in duration, and are not eligible for appeal.
Activision reports: The current policy says players/parties may not earn progression in LMM, and status can later return to normal, recur, or escalate.
Activision reports: Unauthorized memory/content modifications, unsupported cheating peripherals, and identity/hardware spoofing are sanctionable under the policy.
The enforcement policy states that it applies to MW2019 and subsequent COD PC/console titles.
Activision reports: Temporary bans and LMM cannot be appealed; permanent-ban reversal is described as limited to determined account compromise. Hardware-ban status is checked in-game.
Activision reports: The public page says appeal decisions are final and duplicate or alternate-channel submissions will not receive responses.
Activision reports: The PC feature announcement describes server detections, TPM/Secure Boot, investigations, legal pressure, email verification, and 2FA as the launch protection approach.
User-mode applications have separate virtual address spaces and restricted access to OS memory; kernel code runs in the operating system’s privileged context.
Kernel drivers are not isolated from the kernel/other drivers in the way ordinary applications are; a driver fault can crash the OS.
PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx registers callbacks for process creation/exit, providing a documented mechanism for system-level process observation.
Microsoft requires registered process-notify callbacks to be removed before driver unload.
Microsoft documents ObRegisterCallbacks for process, thread, and desktop handle operations.
The callback code must reside in an appropriately signed kernel image; callbacks must be unregistered before unload.
PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine notifies a registered driver when executable images such as DLLs/EXEs are mapped or loaded.
IOCTLs can carry requests between user-mode applications and drivers or between drivers; private vendor codes need not be publicly documented.
Microsoft documents user-mode DeviceIoControl requests being delivered as IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL.
Microsoft’s policy generally requires new kernel drivers to be signed through its developer portal on Windows 10 1607+, with documented legacy exceptions.
Azure’s documented model validates endorsement-key/certificate evidence, then binds an attestation identity key to a trusted TPM.
TPM-backed boot measurements provide evidence for a relying party’s policy evaluation; an attested state depends on what that policy actually checks.
Azure can evaluate measured Secure Boot variables and complementary code-integrity/HVCI/secure-launch evidence; these are platform capabilities, not confirmed COD requirements.
The client collects a TPM quote and TCG boot logs, submits evidence, and receives an attestation token if verification/policy checks succeed.
The relying party validates the attestation token’s signature using service signing metadata before relying on the resulting claims.
Microsoft’s generic TPM workflow includes client authentication to Microsoft Entra ID.
Secure Boot checks trust in boot components; Trusted Boot verifies subsequent OS components; Measured Boot records evidence for later verification.
Microsoft documents DMA-capable peripherals accessing system memory without the CPU performing each read/write.
Windows Kernel DMA Protection uses an IOMMU and device/driver remapping policy to restrict peripheral memory access.
The documented Windows feature needs supporting firmware, does not require VBS, and does not protect the pre-OS boot period.
Microsoft distinguishes device-specific DMA remapping from the overall Kernel DMA Protection policy.
VBS uses the Windows hypervisor for isolation; HVCI/Memory Integrity runs kernel code-integrity enforcement in that isolated environment.
Microsoft says HVCI enforces kernel code integrity in VBS and prevents executable pages from being writable.
Microsoft documents attackers abusing legitimate signed drivers with vulnerabilities; signed code can still create kernel compromise risk.
The vulnerable-driver blocklist is a mitigation, not a guarantee of blocking every vulnerable driver; compatibility affects deployment.
Microsoft documents customer-configurable policies determining attestation-token issuance from evidence.
Azure documents issuing signed JWTs. RFC 7519 distinguishes signatures/integrity protection from encryption.
MmCopyMemory copies physical or virtual memory into a caller buffer. Physical mode excludes I/O space; virtual mode uses system or current-process address space.
Microsoft documents MmCopyMemory returning errors or partial-copy results and the transferred-byte count.
ETW separates event providers, session controllers, and consumers; it supports real-time consumption and file logging.
Microsoft’s protocol distinguishes basic TPM requests from requests also carrying VBS evidence.
The service issues a challenge, and relying-party data can contain a nonce to bind evidence to a fresh attestation request.
Microsoft documents AIK certificates/public keys, boot logs, and current/boot claims as attestation-evidence fields.
AMD documents fTPM 3.*.0.* attestation errors, fixed through firmware delivered to board manufacturers; the bulletin directs users to their motherboard vendor.
AMD notes TPM firmware updates can affect BitLocker recovery; firmware changes should follow the board vendor’s instructions and recovery-key guidance.
Activision reports: The August FAQ explicitly describes the kernel driver monitoring during gameplay and blocking tampering; boot protections complement rather than replace it.
Activision says uninstalling the protected game removes the driver; reinstalling includes it again.
SteamDB’s own detection rules associate the filename Randgrid.sys with Ricochet. A filename alone cannot establish a sample’s authenticity, version, or behavior.
ssno’s article explicitly scopes its analysis to user-mode TAC in Black Ops Cold War.
The ARES paper’s case studies are BattlEye, EAC, FACEIT, and Vanguard.
CODUpdates acknowledged disabling a detection workaround affecting legitimate MWIII/Warzone accounts and said affected accounts were restored.
Call of Duty announced new DMA-cheat detections deployed ahead of that week’s DMZ Early Access.
Call of Duty describes Server Culling as limiting player information sent to clients to make wallhacks harder to use.
The official MW4 week-one post reports suspected-cheating reports trending below the prior year’s launch.
Activision reports: The whitepaper inserts fake entities while serializing server snapshots, before client processing, to avoid changing authoritative gameplay state.
Activision reports: Its chosen method copies a real-player snapshot entry into an unused entry and changes the copy; configurable generators update that decoy’s behavior.
Activision reports: The design must preserve plausible player data, conceal decoys from legitimate observation, remain maintainable/fast, and permit behavior changes.
The Hallucinations paper reports testing accessible feature combinations in three popular cheat programs.
The paper labels position/angle behaviors deployed, Emerge a prototype, and imitation learning possible future work.
The CheckMATE paper evaluates 11 games; its stated experimental period is September–December 2023.
The authors report detecting most non-kernel attempts but no detections in their kernel-based experiments.
The study explicitly excludes advanced server-side defenses such as machine-learning behavioral analysis.
The authors tested in menus and gameplay, allowing two full game lengths for a response where applicable.
The authors say forum data ended in January 2024 and additional protections could have been undisclosed or introduced later.
The authors report no hardware-ID bans in their tests. This records their 2023 observation, not a current ban policy.
The study says it did not test signatures of purchased cheats, disadvantaging systems that enforce only on known-cheat detections.
The research repository’s README states that complete datasets and testing programs are supplied. No testing program was executed here.
Activision identifies CODBrokerInstaller.exe as the default elevated TPM-registration prompt, with enrollaik.exe used in some cases.

text: The parsed bundle manifest has no entry named Randgrid.sys. This utility inspection does not inspect or certify the RICOCHET kernel driver.
Microsoft’s sample demonstrates separate examples of restricting process-handle access and rejecting process creation based on a command-line match.
The sample registers pre/post callbacks for process and thread handle creation and duplication through ObRegisterCallbacks.

Its pre-operation callback selects DesiredAccess for create/duplicate operations and demonstrates clearing termination rights for its protected target. This is sample policy, not a RICOCHET detection specification.
The reject branch checks a process command-line match and sets CreateInfo->CreationStatus to STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED.
The sample unload path unregisters process notifications, removes object-callback filtering, deletes its symbolic link and deletes its device object.
DesiredAccess initially matches OriginalDesiredAccess; a handle pre-operation callback can remove documented access rights but cannot add rights beyond the requested access.
Microsoft lists PROCESS_VM_OPERATION and PROCESS_VM_WRITE among process-handle rights a pre-operation callback may restrict.
Duplicate-handle pre-operation information includes requested/original access and source/target process objects; documented rights can be restricted.
A process-notify callback receives the process object, process ID and optional creation information; NULL CreateInfo indicates process exit.
The image-load callback’s FullImageName can be NULL; ProcessId identifies the target process and is zero for a newly loaded driver.
Microsoft documents image-load callbacks at PASSIVE_LEVEL inside a critical region with normal kernel APCs disabled, and requires callback removal before unload.
METHOD_BUFFERED uses SystemBuffer for both input and output, with separate InputBufferLength and OutputBufferLength limits.
Direct IOCTL methods provide SystemBuffer plus an MDL-described second buffer; IN_DIRECT checks read access and OUT_DIRECT checks write access to that buffer.
METHOD_NEITHER provides user virtual addresses without I/O-manager validation/mapping and supplies no system buffer or MDL.

scope: Windows IOCTL format; not a private vendor command schema
text: CTL_CODE combines device type, access, function and transfer-method fields into a 32-bit IOCTL value.
The IOCTL Access field specifies required device-handle rights; the I/O manager dispatches the request only when the caller requested the specified access.
Microsoft requires dispatch validation of the entire 32-bit IOCTL and input/output lengths, and advises against generic kernel-memory read/write control codes.
IoValidateDeviceIoControlAccess supports stricter dynamic access checks; zeroing driver-allocated output buffers prevents accidental kernel-data disclosure.
Microsoft documents protected kernel code/data whose modification triggers CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION. Kernel privilege does not make those modifications supported.
Microsoft prohibits drivers from using private stacks, modifying IDT/GDT dispatch tables, or modifying undocumented kernel data structures.
Sigcheck reports version/timestamp/signature details; -h displays file hashes and -i displays catalog/signing-chain information.
MmGetSystemRoutineAddress resolves kernel/HAL exports, returning NULL when unresolved; it does not resolve arbitrary driver-defined routines.
PROCESS_VM_READ is required for ReadProcessMemory; PROCESS_VM_WRITE and PROCESS_VM_OPERATION govern documented write/address-space operations.
OpenProcess checks requested rights against the process security descriptor’s DACL. These are OS access checks, not game-content entitlement checks.
Activision states that Warzone progression is stored on the Activision account and continues across linked platforms.
Activision states that progress does not carry over when a platform account is linked to a different Activision account.
Activision states that progress and purchased/earned content in cross-progression games are stored on the Activision account.
The support page distinguishes platform-bound COD Points and real-money purchases from COD-Point content shared across linked accounts, subject to platform exclusives.
